questions.question: From first principles, a data-center network fabric is best described as:
options: A dense multipath interconnect (many equal-cost paths) optimized for scalable east-west connectivity
Only the public internet peering edge
Only a single uplink to one core router
questions.explanation: Fabric = multipath Clos/spine-leaf (or successor) plane under hosts.

questions.question: When the JD says fabrics 'underpin the software services and platforms' in a region, it means:
options: EC2/EBS/S3 and internal platforms depend on that connectivity plane for capacity, low loss, and fast recovery
Fabrics replace the need for any application software
Only DNS is required; fabrics are optional
Customers must configure fabric OSPF themselves
questions.explanation: NFE language: unconstrained connectivity for EC2/EBS/S3-class services.

questions.question: Inside an AWS Region, fabrics matter at which layers?
options: Intra-DC server interconnect plus AZ/DC interconnect so regional services can talk across isolated partitions
Only between continents on the public internet
questions.explanation: Region → AZs/DCs → racks; metro fiber stitches buildings.

questions.question: Classic Clos / spine-leaf exists mainly to solve:
options: Predictable scale-out bandwidth and path diversity for east-west traffic versus hierarchical choke points
Eliminating the need for any routing protocol
Guaranteeing infinite bandwidth with one switch
questions.explanation: Clos theory → modern DC fabric pattern.

questions.question: In AWS networking JD language, 'sustainable' solutions primarily emphasize:
options: Simple, repeatable mechanisms that keep the network healthy as scale grows—not one-off heroics
questions.explanation: NDE JDs: simple/sustainable/repeatable; stability and sustainability of IP networks.

questions.question: Why does network-equipment power matter to fabric sustainability in a data center?
options: Watts used by switches/optics compete with servers; leaner fabrics free power/cooling for more useful capacity
Power is unrelated to rack density
questions.explanation: Amazon Science RNG: fewer routers → less network electricity → more server racks.

questions.question: AWS public research on Resilient Network Graphs (RNG) highlights flatter topologies that aim to:
options: Cut router count and network power while improving throughput/resilience versus classic fat-tree overhead
Require every customer to rewrite apps
questions.explanation: Amazon Science: ~69% fewer routers, ~33% better throughput, ~40% less network electricity projected.

questions.question: Why east-west traffic dominates fabric design pressure in cloud DCs:
options: Services and storage talk constantly inside the DC/AZ—not only north-south to the internet
All traffic is only to the public internet
questions.explanation: Underpinning platforms = heavy internal bandwidth.

questions.question: A healthy regional fabric is 'doing its job' for software platforms when:
options: Service teams get predictable connectivity without caring about Clos/RNG internals
Every app must program spine ASICs
questions.explanation: Underpin = abstraction + reliability underneath APIs.

questions.question: Specialized AI/HPC fabrics vs general-purpose regional fabrics:
options: May use different topologies/protocols optimized for ultra-low latency clusters, while general fabrics still underpin broad regional services
Mean general fabrics no longer matter
questions.explanation: UltraCluster/10p10u vs general Clos/RNG—still one Region, multiple fabric classes.

questions.question: In fabric reliability design, a failure domain is:
options: The set of components that can fail together from one fault—design to limit correlated customer impact
The entire public internet by definition
questions.explanation: Blast-radius thinking for systems that underpin platforms.

questions.question: Two 'redundant' uplinks that share one optical system violate reliability diversity because:
options: A single physical/optical fault can take both paths—redundancy without independence is weak
questions.explanation: Common-mode failure is a classic fabric design miss.

questions.question: N+1 fabric capacity for a failure scenario means:
options: After one planned loss (device/link/spine plane), remaining capacity still meets the designed load/SLO
You only ever need one device
Spare inventory with zero live capacity margin
questions.explanation: Reliability budgeting: design for the failed state, not only the happy path.

questions.question: ECMP improves fabric reliability and scale when:
options: Multiple equal-cost paths exist and hashing spreads load; loss of one path degrades capacity instead of hard isolation
There is only ever one path
It removes need for health checks
questions.explanation: Multipath is foundational to Clos reliability.

questions.question: Graceful degradation for a fabric underpinning services means:
options: Partial failures reduce capacity/latency budget predictably while critical connectivity continues where designed
Any fault immediately blacks out the Region
Silent total loss with no alarms
questions.explanation: Platforms need brownouts they can shed load for—not cliffs.

questions.question: Why must regional fabric design preserve AZ isolation?
options: Software HA assumes independent failure domains; shared fabric fate across AZs defeats multi-AZ architecture
Isolation always reduces performance with no benefit
One shared control plane across all AZs is required
questions.explanation: Underpinning platforms inherit AZ independence requirements.

questions.question: Separating concerns between control plane and data plane reliability matters because:
options: You can sometimes forward on last-known-good state while control recovers—or conversely lose forwarding despite 'green' sessions
They are always identical failure modes
questions.explanation: RIB≠FIB; design and ops must validate both.

questions.question: Gray failures (high loss, corruption, or intermittent faults) are dangerous to platforms because:
options: They cause app timeouts/retries without a clean 'link down' signal—harder detection and longer customer pain
They are always caught by admin-up alone
questions.explanation: Reliability design must detect gray failure, not only hard down.

questions.question: Reliability-oriented fabric observability should include:
options: Loss/latency probes, error/drop counters, utilization, session/neighbor health, and control-plane CPU—not only 'ping the gateway'
questions.explanation: You cannot sustain what you cannot see.

questions.question: A useful reliability SLO for a fabric that underpins platforms might track:
options: Availability/error budget for critical paths (e.g., leaf↔leaf or AZ interconnect) tied to customer-impact minutes
questions.explanation: Error budgets drive change velocity vs risk.

questions.question: Fast reconvergence after a fabric fault is a reliability property because:
options: Customer impact duration ≈ detection + recovery time; slow reconvergence extends brownouts
Faster is always worse for TCP
questions.explanation: BFD/PIC/intent-driven recovery themes at hyperscale.

questions.question: Aggressive failure detection (e.g., very tight BFD) trades off:
options: Faster shift away from dead paths versus false positives/CPU load that can themselves cause instability
questions.explanation: Reliability design is tradeoffs, not max aggressiveness.

questions.question: Before maintenance on a spine/leaf, reliability practice is to:
options: Drain/shift traffic, prove remaining capacity meets SLO, then change with a tested rollback
questions.explanation: Planned failure must look like a designed failure scenario.

questions.question: Canarying fabric automation/config improves reliability by:
options: Limiting blast radius of bad changes and enabling stop/rollback before region-wide impact
Shipping globally faster with no gates
questions.explanation: Change is a top reliability risk at scale.

questions.question: Rollback readiness is part of reliability design because:
options: Mitigation speed during self-inflicted outages dominates customer-impact minutes
Rollback is only for apps, never networks
CI green means rollback is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Bias for Action needs a rehearsed escape hatch.

questions.question: Stacking fiber work + controller deploy + DNS change in one window hurts reliability because:
options: Ambiguous causality and overlapping blast radius slow mitigation
It is always the most efficient plan
questions.explanation: Serialize independent failure domains.

questions.question: Capacity planning for reliability must include failure cases because:
options: Peak+growth on a healthy fabric can still breach SLO after a spine/AZ interconnect loss
Spare ports with no bandwidth math are enough
questions.explanation: Design for N-k load, not only N.

questions.question: Optics/transceiver reliability is first-class in fabric design because:
options: Link flaps and soft failures at high lane speeds drive availability and toil at hyperscale
questions.explanation: Public AWS talks stress optics ownership and reliability.

questions.question: Operationally sustainable cabling (e.g., standardized trunks / ShuffleBox-style patterns) aids reliability by:
options: Reducing misplug rates and speeding correct bring-up/repair under change pressure
Making every path undiverse on purpose
questions.explanation: Human factors are part of reliability design.

questions.question: Control-plane sustainability/reliability at fabric scale requires:
options: Bounded state and reconvergence so failures don't trigger control-plane storms that worsen the outage
Full-mesh flooding of all prefixes with no policy
A single global spanning-tree for the Region
questions.explanation: Why BGP-underlay / intent-driven designs appear.

questions.question: Oversubscription is a reliability-and-cost tradeoff because:
options: Too aggressive oversub causes contention brownouts under hot spots; too little wastes power/capital
questions.explanation: Match fabric oversub to workload + SLO.

questions.question: Unsafe automation is a reliability anti-pattern because:
options: Software multiplies blast radius of mistakes across the fabric faster than manual errors
questions.explanation: Sustainable ops = safe automation.

questions.question: A fabric controller that must be up for all forwarding creates shared fate. Better reliability design:
options: Data plane keeps forwarding on failures where possible; control recovery is independent and staged
Couple every packet to a remote API call
Single global lock for all leaves
questions.explanation: Avoid control-plane as hard dependency for every packet.

questions.question: Network Core software platforms improve fabric reliability when they provide:
options: Validated change pipelines, health signals, auto-remediation with guardrails, and durable RCA fixes
questions.explanation: SysDE plane sustains fabric reliability.

questions.question: Noisy-neighbor / hot-spot effects threaten reliability of platforms on a shared fabric when:
options: A few elephant flows or incast patterns congest shared ECMP members and raise latency/loss for others
questions.explanation: Design: headroom, hashing awareness, isolation where needed.

questions.question: Reliability design for new fabric capacity includes pre-production validation because:
options: You must prove paths, failover, and performance before customer workloads depend on it
Production is the only acceptable testbed always
questions.explanation: Bring-up assurance is reliability engineering.

questions.question: Game days / failure injection on fabric tooling or drains help reliability by:
options: Revealing detection gaps, runbook holes, and wrong capacity assumptions before real Sevs
questions.explanation: Practice the failed state.

questions.question: After a fabric-impacting incident, reliability improves sustainably when:
options: COE actions change mechanisms (guards, tests, topology, alarms)—not only 'be more careful'
The same bug class is accepted as normal
questions.explanation: Highest Standards: defects stay fixed.

questions.question: Refresh/turndown (life-cycle) reliability means:
options: Move traffic safely, decommission without shared-fate surprises, and keep intended state truthful
Yank gear during peaks for speed
questions.explanation: DCLC-style operational excellence.

questions.question: AZ/DC interconnect (metro) reliability design should assume:
options: Diverse fiber/paths and failure scenarios—campus cuts are real and must not collapse multi-AZ software HA
A single conduit is fine forever
questions.explanation: Regional platforms span buildings.

questions.question: Intent-driven / declarative fabric operations improve reliability when:
options: Desired state is reviewable, continuously reconciled, and divergences are detected before customers feel them
questions.explanation: Public AWS networking culture: intent, shift, validate.

questions.question: During a fabric brownout underpinning platforms, reliability operations prioritize:
options: Customer-impact clarity, mitigate/shift first, then Dive Deep—with timed stakeholder updates
questions.explanation: Customer Obsession under partial failure.

questions.question: Dual-homing critical hosts/services to diverse fabric leaves helps when:
options: Leaf/ToR failure does not isolate the workload—and upstream diversity is real, not paper redundancy
Both NICs share one leaf and one uplink
Ignoring switch software bugs that hit both
questions.explanation: Host attachment is part of fabric reliability design.

questions.question: Best SDM STAR for fabric reliability + sustainability:
options: Mechanism that reduced blast radius, impact minutes, or unsafe toil—with baselines and durable follow-through
A one-off CLI hero moment with no mechanism
questions.explanation: Deliver Results + Ownership + Highest Standards.
